commits.message:
A seam's colours read past the seam, and a segment is one colour however a cell carries it (rich-unfiled-791c.uy67)

Review (high, the second) on the region model. Four findings built:

A seam cell's colours took the region in the column right beside it, so a
two-cell rail's inner cell found only the rail's other cell and fell to a
place of its own, out of hue with the item it caps. Each colour now reads
past every seam column to the region beside the seam.

The docs defined a segment as two kinds — on a fill, or in an ink on the
terminal's ground — while the code keyed regions on the colour alone, so a
caption in a bar's colour touching the bar merged with it. The code is the
right one: matching colours a designer placed touching stay matching. The
docs and comments now say a segment is one colour of the element's,
carried as a cell's ground or, on the terminal's ground, as its ink.

`segmentOf` said it was the segment a colour turns with; since the first
review commit it only names the colour a colour's bounds are kept under,
and `segmentsOf` decides where it turns. It is `boundWith` now, and says so.

`segmentsOf` destructured `all` off a `Drawn` and called it detached, which
a class implementing the interface would throw on. It takes the `Drawn`.

Rejected: the per-frame cost for the third time, on the measurement in
the first review comment; a one-colour seam between two segments of its
colour, which can match one side only; and a zero-width glyph pacing with
the glyph at its column, which is the right answer for a cell that is not
on screen.

A wheel segment is a region of one fill, and only a joiner's seam caps (rich-unfiled-791c.uy67)

Review (medium) on the previous commit. Three findings built:

A segment was a run of cells in one row, so a panel's solid ground was
twenty segments banding into a vertical rainbow at the catalogue's swing,
and a row with one highlighted cell on it broke into two regions turning
apart from the rows beside them. A segment is now a region of adjacent
cells, beside or above one another, of one own fill — on the terminal's
ground, one own ink — found by union-find over the covered columns; its
place is the region's centre row and centre column. Strips are the one-row
case and are unchanged: a seam still splits items.

The cap rule applied to any ink that was a fill, so the first letter of a
label in a neighbour's fill colour, abutting that neighbour, turned with
the neighbour and the rest of the word with its own ground. A seam's
colours are its neighbours' edges, so the rule is now the seam's: each
colour of a cell a joiner drew turns with the region of that colour beside
it; any other cell's colours turn with the region covering it.

The prose said a grown run moves "nothing else's" hue; in a strip it pushes
every run to its right along by a column, and each moves as little. The
docs and comments say that now.

Two one-source fixes from the same pass: `WalkedGlyph` carries the width
the walk stepped by, so a listed cell's width is the walk's and not a
second `cellLen`; and `Look` carries `seam`, decided once in `looks`, where
the listing and the word measure both read it.

The wheel reads its runs off every cell the element draws, blanks included (rich-unfiled-791c.uy67)

Review (high) found that a run was read off `Drawn.cells()`, the listing of
cells that show something, so a styled sentence on the terminal's ground
broke into a run per word at every space: measured at the catalogue's
swing, adjacent words of one red sentence differed by a median 19 degrees
and up to 84. The same unlisted blanks each turned their unseen ink at a
place of their own, a full choose per blank per frame: 2000 of them cost
15-23 ms a frame against 2 ms for one run.

`Drawn` now lists every cell the element draws in `all()`, each with its
width, pair and whether a joiner drew it; `cells()` is the shown subset of
that one listing, as before, for the transitions. The wheel reads its runs
off `all()`, so a blank carrying the ink keeps the sentence one run and a
blank in the terminal's ink splits it, and the blanks share their run's
one written colour.

Also from the review: the per-frame memo of written colours is keyed by
the bounds' key with the place, so one entry never serves two bounds; the
comment on the stray's noise offsets states the mechanism that holds (the
`y` offsets' fractions are ones no half-integer centre reaches, so no
sample sits on a lattice line along `t`), and the bounds' header no longer
says a frame writes a colour one way.

The wheel paces each segment by where it sits, not by its colour (rich-unfiled-791c.uy67)

Brandon, via cc-candybar: the wheel should affect segments by their
location, some turning faster than others. The wheel seeded each segment's
stray from a hash of its fill hex, so two segments of one fill kept step
wherever they sat. Now a segment is a run of adjacent cells in one row on
one own fill (on the terminal's ground, in one own ink), its place is the
run's row and centre column from the element's left edge, and the stray's
noise is sampled at that place over STRAY_SPREAD columns a unit: neighbours
pace a little apart, distant runs on their own, and a run that grows by a
column moves its hue a little. The shared turn keeps no place term, since a
place-scaled turn would jump a growing run by 360·t·Δ/P without bound.

Drawn.cells() lists a ListedCell: the Placed cell with the columns its glyph
takes, its on-screen pair, and whether a joiner drew it, read off the one
look and walk the cell is handed with, so the wheel reads its runs from the
frame's own measure. A cap's ink turns at the place of the adjacent run of
its fill, so a powerline cap keeps its run's colour, hand-drawn or a custom
joiner's; a strip's own seams are re-derived from their neighbours as
before. Contrast bounds stay keyed by colour and fill.

0.26.0: a public type gains fields.

gradientSeam draws a monotone ramp under the lift (rich-joiners-er38.a1h) (#517)

* gradientSeam fills each cell with one colour, so the lift moves none and the ramp never turns back (rich-joiners-er38.a1h)

Each cell was a half block carrying two ramp samples, ink over ground. The
lift holds every seam cell's ink at least SEAM_MIN_DELTA_E off its ground,
so wherever two neighbouring samples sat closer than that (near grounds, or
far grounds across many steps, as in rich-strip's full-width fill) every
ink sample was moved and the ramp zig-zagged.

A ramp cell is now a space whose fg is "ground": one colour, its fill,
sampled at the cell's middle. Ink in the terminal's ground is a side the
lift cannot measure, so it moves none of them, by the rule every seam cell
passes. The glyph and ASCII forms are the same ramp.

* Version 0.25.2 (rich-joiners-er38.a1h)

* gradientSeam refuses a step count that is no whole number of cells, and says why a ramp between alike grounds shows no join (rich-joiners-er38.a1h)

* gradientSeam draws no cells for 0 steps, where the items meet, and refuses only a count that is no whole number (rich-joiners-er38.a1h)

* gradientSeam refuses 0 steps, which would join a colourless neighbour without its caps, and the ramp test holds a channel the grounds share still (rich-joiners-er38.a1h)

* A gradientSeam ramp follows the grounds an effect leaves beside it, and becomes their one colour when an effect paints both alike (rich-joiners-er38.a1h)
